body.stem: You have 12 Linux virtual machines whose guest performance counters are collected by a VM insights data collection rule. When you open the multi-VM Performance view in Azure Monitor, the CPU and memory charts are empty, even though the machines are healthy and running. You need the fleet charts to populate from the counters that are already being collected. Which change should you make?

rows: Log Analytics workspaces in the tenant
Workspace currently selected in the Performance view
Data collection rule target for the 12 virtual machines

options.text: Change the Workspace selector to law-central.
Change the Workspace selector to law-secondary.
Change the Group selector so the results include only the resource groups hosting the virtual machines whose data collection rule targets law-central.
Change the TimeRange selector so the charts cover a wider period than the current last-hour range.

explanation.correct: The Workspace selector in the multi-VM Performance view picks the Log Analytics workspace that holds the solution, and the guest counters for these machines are written to law-central by their data collection rule. Because the view is currently pointed at law-secondary, the charts come back empty; pointing the Workspace selector at law-central makes the collected counters appear.

perChoice.b: law-secondary is the workspace already selected, and it is neither where the solution is enabled nor where these machines' data collection rule delivers their counters, so reselecting it leaves the charts empty.
perChoice.c: The Group selector filters by subscriptions, resource groups, computer groups and scale sets, but it does not change which workspace is queried. Narrowing the scope while the wrong workspace is selected still returns no guest performance counters.
perChoice.d: The TimeRange selector only sets the period that is displayed, and the default is the last hour. Widening the window cannot surface counters that were never written to the workspace being queried.

body.stem: You track the service availability of your Azure Storage accounts with Storage insights, and the configuration currently applied to the availability workbook is listed below. Your operations team needs any account whose availability falls below 85% to be reported with the Critical health state, while the Warning state must still be raised at 99% availability. Which change should you make?

options.text: In the Availability (%) (Thresholds + Formatted) column settings, set the minimum value to 85 and leave the maximum value at 99.
In the Availability (%) (Thresholds + Formatted) column settings, set the maximum value to 85 and leave the minimum value at 90.
In the Availability (%) (Thresholds + Formatted) column settings, set the minimum value to 99 and the maximum value to 85.
In the Availability (%) (Thresholds + Formatted) column settings, set the minimum value to 85 and the maximum value to 85.

explanation.correct: The availability thresholds in this workbook are configured as a minimum/maximum pair that ships as minimum 90 and maximum 99, producing Warning at 99% and Critical at 90%. The Critical health state is raised only when availability drops below the minimum value, and the value you edit for the Critical state is that minimum. Changing the minimum to 85 while keeping the maximum at 99 therefore makes an account critical below 85% and leaves the warning level at 99%. (In practice you switch the workbook to Edit mode, edit the Availability (%) (Thresholds + Formatted) column in the Availability by API name grid, then Save as and Done editing so the published default is not overwritten.)

perChoice.b: The maximum value of the pair corresponds to the warning level, not to the critical boundary, and the critical state fires only below the minimum value. Changing the maximum to 85 moves the warning threshold while the critical boundary stays at 90%, so an account at 87% would still not be reported as critical.
perChoice.c: This swaps the two bounds, so the critical state would be raised only below 99% and the warning level would move down to 85%. That does not produce a critical state below 85% and changes the warning level in the wrong direction.
perChoice.d: Setting both values to 85 does move the critical boundary to 85%, but it also pulls the warning level down from 99% to 85%, so accounts between 85% and 99% would be flagged as warning and the requirement that warning still trigger at 99% is not satisfied.

body.stem: Your virtual machine fleet is spread across the resource groups shown below. You must hand the operations team a ranking of every machine in the fleet by CPU utilization, so the worst performers can be worked through one at a time. Which should you do?

options.text: Open the Top N List tab of the multi-VM Performance view and use its Load More control, which can extend the ranking to 500 machines.
Open the Top N Charts tab of the multi-VM Performance view and read the CPU Utilization % chart, which ranks the five machines with the highest values.
Open the Aggregated Charts tab of the multi-VM Performance view and read the CPU Utilization % chart, which shows average and 95th percentile values across the fleet.
Open the Top N List tab of the multi-VM Performance view and switch the Metric dropdown to Network Received Byte/s, which reveals every machine in the fleet.

explanation.correct: The Top N List tab of the multi-VM Performance view opens with the 20 highest-ranked machines, ranked by 95th-percentile CPU Utilization %, and its Load More control extends that ranking to as many as 500 machines. Your fleet holds 300 virtual machines (180 + 70 + 50), so expanding the ranking once covers every machine and gives the operations team the complete CPU ordering they asked for.

perChoice.b: The Top N Charts tab is a quick five-machine comparison: it shows CPU Utilization %, Available Memory, Logical Disk Space Used %, Bytes Sent Rate and Bytes Receive Rate, and each of those charts lists only its own top five machines. It is useful for spotting outliers at a glance but cannot produce a ranking of a 300-machine fleet.
perChoice.c: Aggregated Charts summarises the fleet rather than ranking individual machines: CPU Utilization % and Logical Disk Space Used % default to average plus the 95th percentile, and Available Memory defaults to average, 5th and 10th percentile. No per-machine ordering of all 300 machines is available there.
perChoice.d: The Metric dropdown in the Top N List only changes which signal the machines are ranked by - Available Memory, Logical Disk Space Used %, Network Received Byte/s or Network Sent Byte/s. It does not change how many machines the ranking shows, and ranking by received bytes would not answer a CPU utilization request in any case.

body.stem: You are troubleshooting the network traffic of a single virtual machine, and the two network charts in the table below disagree about how many bytes the machine sent in the last hour. You need to know which of the two figures reflects the traffic this VM exchanges with the other VMs in the same virtual network. Which statement explains the difference?

columns: Bytes sent in the last hour
rows: Network chart on the Azure VM overview page
Bytes Sent Rate chart on the VM insights Performance tab

options.text: The overview chart is measured by the host and shows only billable traffic, while VM insights measures inside the guest and includes traffic between VMs.
The overview chart is measured inside the guest and includes traffic between VMs, while VM insights is measured by the host and shows only billable traffic.
Both charts are measured by the host, but the overview chart excludes traffic between VMs while VM insights includes it.
Both charts are measured inside the guest, and the difference comes from the sampling interval used to collect the counters.

explanation.correct: The network chart on the Azure VM overview page is drawn from the host's view of activity in the guest machine and covers only the traffic that gets billed, so traffic exchanged with other VMs in the virtual network never appears there. The VM insights Performance charts come from counters collected inside the guest VM itself and account for all inbound and outbound TCP/IP traffic, including inter-VM traffic. That is why the guest-based figure (48.7 GB) is far larger than the overview figure (12.4 GB), and why VM insights is the chart to trust for traffic between VMs.

perChoice.b: This reverses the two data sources. The overview page chart is the host-measured one that shows only billed traffic and omits inter-VM traffic, while VM insights is the guest-measured chart that includes it.
perChoice.c: This mixes up the two charts. VM insights is not host-measured; its data is gathered inside the guest VM. The gap between the two figures comes from what the overview chart counts (billed traffic only), not from two charts taken at the same measurement point.
perChoice.d: This is wrong because the overview chart is host-measured rather than guest-measured, and the difference is not caused by sampling intervals. It comes from the scope of the data each chart counts: billed traffic only versus all inbound and outbound traffic including inter-VM traffic.

body.stem: You have a storage account whose failures view reports only three named error types and pushes every other error into one mixed category, as shown below. Your support team needs the six most significant error types to appear as separate entries, while the remaining transactions are still summarized in their own group, because a rare error type is currently hidden inside that mixed bucket. Which change should you make?

rows: Combined under a single category named Other (5,742 transactions)

options.text: Set the Number of Splits to 7 so that six error types are listed separately and the remaining errors are still reported in their own group
Set the Number of Splits to 6 so that six error types are listed separately and the remaining errors are still reported in their own group
Set the Number of Splits to 8 so that six error types are listed separately and the remaining errors are still reported in their own group
Set the Number of Splits to 5 so that six error types are listed separately and the remaining errors are still reported in their own group

explanation.correct: The failures view breaks out only three error types and merges the rest into the Other category because the split limit on the error metric is 3. The split value reserves one slot for the remainder of the errors, so the value that surfaces n distinct named error types is n + 1. To get six named error types while still keeping the leftover transactions summarized in their own group, the Number of Splits must be set to 7 (six named types plus the remainder slot). You make this change by editing the workbook, opening the metric's parameters (Transactions, Sum) and changing Number of Splits.

perChoice.b: This value leaves no slot for the remainder: one of the splits is consumed by the grouped remainder, so only five error types are actually broken out and one of the types you need is still merged into the mixed category.
perChoice.c: This value reserves one split for the remainder but breaks out seven named error types rather than six, so it lists more categories than you asked for and the extra named type displaces one of the types you wanted to see.
perChoice.d: This value is one below what is needed: only four error types are broken out, so two of the types your team needs are still merged into the remainder group and remain hidden.

body.stem: You have an operations team of six analysts who must read the guest performance counters of the virtual machines in your fleet from the Azure Monitor multi-VM Performance view. Their current role assignments are listed below. Which change should you make?

options.text: Assign Monitoring Reader on the virtual machine and on the VM insights data collection rule
Assign Reader on the virtual machine and on the VM insights data collection rule
Assign Monitoring Reader on the Log Analytics workspace that receives the performance data
Assign Monitoring Reader on the virtual machine only

explanation.correct: Reading VM performance data requires the Monitoring Reader role on the virtual machine and on the VM insights data collection rule (DCR). The analysts currently hold only Reader at the resource group scope, with no assignment on either the virtual machine or the data collection rule, so granting Monitoring Reader on both of those scopes is what lets them read the guest performance counters.

perChoice.b: Reader is not the role that grants access to VM performance data; the documented requirement is the Monitoring Reader role on the virtual machine and on the VM insights data collection rule, so keeping Reader on those scopes leaves the team unable to read the counters.
perChoice.c: Assigning the role only on the Log Analytics workspace leaves the required access on the virtual machine and on the VM insights data collection rule in place, so the performance data still cannot be read by the team.
perChoice.d: The role is also required on the VM insights data collection rule, so granting Monitoring Reader on the virtual machine alone satisfies only one of the two required scopes.

body.stem: You have 480 storage accounts spread across three subscriptions, and the operations team wants a single view of their availability, latency and errors from the storage Overview workbook in Azure Monitor. You widen the scope selector so that all three subscriptions are in scope. Which statement correctly describes what the workbook will show you?

options.text: At most 200 of the accounts appear in the workbook, so the remaining accounts have to be reviewed in separate batches.
All 480 accounts appear in the workbook, because adding the subscriptions to the scope removes any cap on the account count.
Only 15 accounts appear, because the five accounts chosen per subscription are fixed and cannot be changed.
600 accounts appear, because the maximum of 200 applies to each of the three subscriptions separately.

explanation.correct: The storage Overview workbook opens with about five accounts per subscription pre-selected, and expanding the scope selector returns up to 200 accounts in total. Because your three subscriptions hold 480 accounts, the workbook shows no more than 200 of them and the rest have to be worked through in further passes.

perChoice.b: Widening the scope selector does not remove the cap on how many accounts are returned; the selection tops out at 200 accounts, so all 480 can never be listed in one pass.
perChoice.c: The five accounts per subscription are only the default selection that is preselected when the workbook opens. Choosing more in the scope selector goes well beyond that default, so 15 is not the result of selecting all three subscriptions.
perChoice.d: The 200-account maximum applies to the selection as a whole rather than to each subscription individually, so three subscriptions do not multiply it into 600 rows.

body.stem: You have a Linux virtual machine whose guest counters are collected by VM insights, and you are reviewing the logical disk charts for the file systems mounted on it. As shown below, one mount reports values while the other never does. You need the capacity team to understand why the second mount produces no disk data. Which statement correctly explains this behavior?

rows: Managed data disk attached to the VM
Azure Files SMB share mounted from the network

options.text: On Linux VMs, guest disk counters are collected only from local data disks using XFS or the EXT family, and network shared drives are excluded.
On Linux VMs, guest disk counters are collected only from local data disks using NTFS or the EXT family, and network shared drives are excluded.
On Linux VMs, guest disk counters are collected from every mounted volume, including network shared drives, as soon as the machine reports to Azure Monitor.
On Linux VMs, guest disk counters are collected only from local data disks using XFS or the EXT family, and network shared drives are included as well.

explanation.correct: VM insights gathers guest disk counters on Linux only from attached data disks that use XFS or an EXT filesystem (EXT2, EXT3, EXT4), and it does not sample file systems served from remote shares. The /mnt/data mount is an attached XFS data disk, which is why its charts populate, while /mnt/share is an SMB mount from Azure Files, so no counters are ever produced for it.

perChoice.b: NTFS is not one of the file systems that yield guest disk counters on Linux. The attached XFS data disk is exactly the kind of volume that does produce values, so this statement contradicts the populated chart for /mnt/data.
perChoice.c: Remote network shares do not contribute guest disk counters, and simply reporting to Azure Monitor does not change that. The empty chart for /mnt/share shows the volume is never sampled, so this statement cannot explain the result.
perChoice.d: Network shared drives stay out of disk counter collection on Linux, so the CIFS-backed Azure Files mount cannot supply the missing values. This statement contradicts the chart that shows nothing for /mnt/share.

body.stem: You support the estate shown below, and the six requests below keep arriving from the operations team. Drag each request to the Azure Monitor page or the Network insights view that answers it.

rows: 38 Windows and Linux servers across three subscriptions; guest counters are collected by a VM insights data collection rule
110 storage accounts in two subscriptions, plus one account under investigation for a latency incident
Load balancer, application gateway, NAT gateway and six network security groups spread over two VNets

items.text: Monitor > Insights > Storage Accounts
Monitor > Solutions > Virtual Machines > Performance
Storage account > Monitoring > Insights
Network insights > Traffic tab
Network insights > Connectivity tab
Network insights > Diagnostic Toolkit

slots.label: Compare service health, response times and error counts for every data service across all of your subscriptions
One screen showing the busiest processors and the least free memory for all of the servers in your fleet
Drill into a single resource to review its errors, response times, service health and space usage
Turn on and confirm the flow records and analytics that your network security groups send
Watch reachability test results and set the criteria that decide each outcome
Trace the next hop, confirm an allow or deny decision and capture packets

explanation.correct: Each request maps to the surface that is built for it: the multi-account entry point under Monitor > Insights > Storage Accounts compares availability, latency and errors across subscriptions; the multi-machine Performance view under Monitor > Solutions > Virtual Machines shows guest CPU and memory counters for a whole fleet; the per-account Monitoring > Insights page holds the Failures, Performance, Availability and Capacity workbooks for one account; the Network insights Traffic tab lists the network security groups and shows their NSG flow log and Traffic analytics configuration status, which is where those settings are configured; the Connectivity tab lists the Connection monitor tests with their reachability status and exposes the criteria (checks failed % and RTT) that determine that status; and the Diagnostic Toolkit provides next hop, IP flow verify, packet capture, connection troubleshoot and VPN troubleshoot for acting on a suspected network problem.

perChoice.a: Belongs with the request to compare service health, response times and error counts for every data service across all subscriptions: this is the cross-subscription entry point that compares many accounts on availability, latency and errors.
perChoice.b: Belongs with the request for one screen of the busiest processors and least free memory for the whole fleet: this is the multi-machine Performance view that charts guest counters for VMs across work groups and subscriptions.
perChoice.c: Belongs with the request to drill into a single resource: this is where the Failures, Performance, Availability and Capacity workbooks for one account live, so errors, response times, service health and space usage for that account are reviewed here.
perChoice.d: Belongs with the request about the flow records and analytics sent by network security groups: the Traffic tab lists the NSGs in scope and shows which ones have NSG flow logs and Traffic analytics configured, and that configuration is edited from the flowlog configuration status column.
perChoice.e: Belongs with the request about reachability test results and the criteria behind them: the Connectivity tab visualizes the Connection monitor tests and their reachability status, and the criteria you set (checks failed % and RTT ms) immediately change each test's outcome.
perChoice.f: Belongs with the request to trace the next hop, confirm an allow or deny decision and capture packets: these are the diagnostic actions (next hop, IP flow verify, packet capture) exposed by the toolkit, which is where you act rather than only read.

body.stem: You support 120 Azure Storage accounts that are watched with Storage insights, and your team answers every customer ticket from the four workbooks that sit on a single account's Monitoring > Insights page. The account below is the subject of four open tickets. Drag each ticket to the workbook that answers it.

rows: Average time spent handling a request inside the service
Requests answered with an error status
Share of the allotted space in use
Data objects stored in the account

items.text: Ticket 4812 — The customer wants to know whether a regional problem affected the storage service during last night's incident, and how the state of each data service in the account has changed across the selected window.
Ticket 4823 — The customer says their calls are slow and wants the end-to-end time compared with the time the service itself spent handling each request.
Ticket 4830 — The customer wants a breakdown of the responses their application received with an error status, including how many of those were throttled.
Ticket 4841 — The customer wants to know how much of the allotted space is in use and how many data objects the account is holding.

explanation.correct: Each ticket asks for a different category of information, and each account-level workbook in Storage insights is tailored to one category. The request about a regional incident and the state of each data service over the selected window belongs with the Availability workbook, which opens with the health state of the storage service and shows a per-data-service trend line and trend chart. The request comparing end-to-end time with the time spent inside the service belongs with the Performance workbook, whose rollup tile and chart set contrast E2E latency with server latency and break latency of successful calls down by API. The request about error responses and throttled requests belongs with the Failures workbook, which carries tiles for client-side errors other than the named ones and for client-throttling errors plus tables of transactions by API name and by response type. The request about space in use and the number of objects held belongs with the Capacity workbook, which reports the amount of storage used per data object and how many data objects are stored.

perChoice.t4812: It asks whether a regional problem hit the service and how each data service has trended over the window, which is what the Availability workbook shows: the current health state of Azure Storage, the health state of each object categorized by data service, and a trend line and chart per data service for the selected time range.
perChoice.t4823: It compares the total time a request takes end to end with the time the service itself spends on it, which is the E2E-versus-server-latency comparison and the successful-call latency breakdown by API that the Performance workbook provides.
perChoice.t4830: It asks about client-side error responses and throttled requests, which the Failures workbook reports through its tiles for other client errors and client-throttling errors and its transactions-by-API-name and transactions-by-response-type tables.
perChoice.t4841: It asks how much space is in use and how many objects are held, which the Capacity workbook reports as the amount of storage used for each storage data object and how many data objects are stored in the account.

body.stem: You have 240 virtual machines onboarded to VM insights, and the on-call team raises the same three requests during every shift. You need each request answered from the multi-VM Performance view (Monitor > Solutions > Virtual Machines > Performance). Which tab should each request go to? Drag each request to the correct tab.

items.text: Show the five machines under the heaviest processor load and the five with the least free memory side by side, so the shift can eyeball the whole fleet in seconds.
Rank every machine in the fleet by available memory and keep extending the ranking until all of them are included, so the worst offender can be handed to a capacity owner.
Report the fleet-wide mean and 95th percentile of file system space consumed, so a single number can be trended week over week.

explanation.correct: The three requests map one-to-one onto the three tabs of the multi-VM Performance view. The quick side-by-side glance at the five busiest machines by processor load and the five with the least free memory belongs to Top N Charts, because that tab renders five charts (CPU Utilization %, Available Memory, Logical Disk Space Used %, Bytes Sent Rate, Bytes Receive Rate) and each chart shows only its top five machines. The request to rank every individual machine and work through them one by one belongs to Top N List: it opens with 20 machines ordered by 95th-percentile CPU Utilization %, the Load More button extends the ranking up to 500 machines, and the Metric dropdown switches the ranking to Available Memory, so all 240 machines in the fleet can be covered. The request for a fleet-wide mean and 95th percentile of file system space consumed belongs to Aggregated Charts, which reports averages and percentiles across many machines and defaults Logical Disk Space Used % to average plus the 95th percentile.

perChoice.item1: Belongs in Top N Charts. That tab draws five charts - CPU Utilization %, Available Memory, Logical Disk Space Used %, Bytes Sent Rate and Bytes Receive Rate - and each chart carries only its top five machines, which is exactly the at-a-glance side-by-side view the request describes.
perChoice.item2: Belongs in Top N List. It is the view for finding which individual machine trends worst: it starts with 20 machines ranked by 95th-percentile CPU Utilization %, the Load More button extends the ranking to a maximum of 500 machines, and the Metric dropdown changes the ranking to Available Memory, so the full fleet of 240 machines can be worked through one at a time.
perChoice.item3: Belongs in Aggregated Charts. This tab reports fleet-wide values rather than per-machine rankings, and Logical Disk Space Used % defaults to average plus the 95th percentile, matching the requested mean and 95th-percentile figure.

body.stem: You support the production estate listed below, and the operations team raises the same four kinds of requests every week. Everything is answered from the Network insights page in Azure Monitor, but each request has to be handled in the specific area of that page that holds the data or the controls needed to answer it. Drag each request to the correct area.

rows: Flow log and analytics collection configured
cm-branch (reachability test to the branch office)
Calls to a partner API take about 8 seconds

items.text: Give me the inventory of the resources deployed in the production resource group, each type counted and sorted by name, and let a search for a public IP address also return the resources attached to it.
Work out which of the network security groups in the subscription are not publishing flow logs, and switch the collection on for those that are missing.

Check whether the reachability tests between the branch office and the virtual network are passing, and tighten the criteria for failed checks percentage and round-trip time so that a degraded link is reported sooner.
Find out why calls to a partner API from one virtual machine are slow: capture the packets that leave the machine and confirm the next hop along the route.

explanation.correct: Each request belongs to the area of Network insights that carries its data or its controls. The inventory of deployed resources — filtered by subscription, resource group and type, sorted by name or resource count, with a search box that also returns associated resources — is the Network health area, which answers the request about a public IP address and the resources attached to it. The list of network security groups with their flow log configuration status, where the missing collection can be turned on, is the Traffic area. The results of the configured tests together with the criteria that decide their verdict (checks failed percentage and round-trip time) are the Connectivity area. The troubleshooting tools used to capture packets and confirm the next hop for one slow virtual machine are the Diagnostic Toolkit.

perChoice.inv: This belongs in the Network health area: that area filters the deployed resources by subscription, resource group and type, sorts them by name or resource count, and its search box returns associated resources, so a public IP address search also returns the application gateway attached to it.
perChoice.nsg: This belongs in the Traffic area: that area lists the network security groups of the selected subscriptions, resource groups and locations, flags which of them already publish flow logs and analytics, and exposes the configuration status column used to enable the missing collection.
perChoice.reach: This belongs in the Connectivity area: that area shows the reachability status of the configured tests and lets you set the criteria (checks failed percentage and round-trip time) whose values immediately change whether each test is reported as reachable.
perChoice.pkt: This belongs in the Diagnostic Toolkit area: it is the drop-down list of troubleshooting features such as packet capture and next hop, used to inspect the packets leaving a single virtual machine and the path they take.

body.stem: You support a storage estate and a fleet of virtual machines that the operations team watches with Azure Monitor. The requests below keep arriving, and each request has to be handled in one specific place, control, or chart. Drag each request to the place, control, or chart that answers it.

rows: Resource group holding the customized copies
Virtual machines watched with VM insights

items.text: Keep a private copy of the customized availability view that only the person who made the changes can open.
Publish the customized availability view so every colleague who has access to the resource group can open it.
Create a second copy of the published default and leave the version that ships with the product untouched.
See at a glance the total number of accounts covered and how many of them are currently selected.
Hand the used-capacity figures to the capacity manager in a file they can open outside the portal.
Show how many read and write operations each volume performed on a single virtual machine.

explanation.correct: Each request resolves to one element of the Storage insights workbooks or to a chart on the per-virtual-machine performance page: a customized copy that only its creator can open lives under My Reports, a copy for everyone with access to the resource group lives under Shared Reports, a separate copy of the published default is created with Save as, the running totals of accounts covered and selected come from the counter tile, the Overview and Capacity workbooks can be exported to Excel, and the per-volume read/write activity chart on one virtual machine is Logical Disk IOPS.

perChoice.a: Customized workbooks are stored in a resource group either in My Reports, which is private to the person who created it, or in Shared Reports. A copy that only the person who made the changes can open belongs under My Reports.
perChoice.b: Shared Reports is the section of the resource group that everyone with access to that resource group can open, so a customized availability view intended for the whole team belongs there.
perChoice.c: Customizations never overwrite the published default workbook. Choosing Save as creates a copy of the workbook with the customizations, leaving the shipped default unchanged.
perChoice.d: The counter tile that sits under the drop-down lists rolls up the total number of storage accounts in scope and reflects how many of them are selected.
perChoice.e: The multi-subscription and account-level Overview and Capacity workbooks support exporting the results in Excel format by selecting the down arrow icon next to the pushpin icon.
perChoice.f: The performance page of a single virtual machine adds Logical Disk IOPS, Logical Disk MB/s and Max Logical Disk Used % to the chart set, so the read and write operation activity of each logical disk is reported by Logical Disk IOPS.

body.stem: You look after a storage estate that is monitored with Storage insights, and the storage platform team sends the same requests in every reporting cycle. You need each request handled in one specific place or control of the Azure Monitor storage experience. Drag each request to where it belongs.

items.text: A copy of the availability workbook that only I will ever see.
A copy of the capacity workbook that everyone on the storage platform team can open.
Find where the copy of the failures workbook I saved this morning is kept.
A spreadsheet with the figures from the multi-subscription Overview and Capacity workbooks.
Launch the customized copy of the Overview workbook that I saved last week.

slots.label: the storage account that was open when the copy was made
the down arrow next to the pushpin

explanation.correct: Customized copies of the storage workbooks are saved in a resource group in one of two sections: My Reports, which is private to the person who created the copy, and Shared Reports, which everyone with access to that resource group can open. That is why the availability copy that only one person may see belongs under My Reports, while the capacity copy for the whole storage platform team belongs under Shared Reports. Where a copy physically lives is a separate matter: each saved workbook is kept inside the storage account that was open when it was saved, which is where the failures workbook nobody can find has to be looked. The multi-subscription and account-level Overview and Capacity workbooks produce a spreadsheet file through the down arrow icon next to the pushpin, and a copy that has already been saved is opened from the workbook gallery.

perChoice.a: My Reports is the section of the resource group that holds customized copies private to the person who made them, which matches a copy that only its creator will ever open. Shared Reports would expose it to everyone with access to the resource group.
perChoice.b: Shared Reports is the section that everyone with access to the resource group can open, so a capacity copy meant for the whole storage platform team belongs there. My Reports would keep that copy visible only to its creator, and neither the gallery nor the export icon deals with sharing a copy.
perChoice.c: Every saved workbook is kept in the storage account that was open at the moment it was saved, so the copy that nobody can find has to be tracked down inside that account. My Reports and Shared Reports describe how widely a copy may be opened rather than which account holds it, and the gallery is only used to launch a copy whose location is already known.
perChoice.d: The multi-subscription and account-level Overview and Capacity workbooks can be exported to Excel by selecting the down arrow icon next to the pushpin, which is what produces the requested spreadsheet. My Reports and Shared Reports store customized copies, and the gallery launches workbooks, so none of them delivers a spreadsheet file.
perChoice.e: After a customized workbook has been saved with Save as, it is launched from the workbook gallery. My Reports and Shared Reports are storage locations for copies rather than the place you open them from, and the down arrow next to the pushpin exports grid results instead of opening a saved copy.

body.stem: You look after 210 Linux virtual machines whose guest counters reach a single Log Analytics workspace through a VM insights data collection rule. The capacity team has asked for one picture that covers the whole fleet and makes the machines closest to exhausting their memory visible. You open the multi-VM Performance view (Monitor > Solutions > Virtual Machines > Performance) to build it. Which tab do you take the chart from, and what does the memory chart on that tab show by default?

rows: How much memory each machine still has available
One chart covering the whole fleet, not a list of individual machines
The smallest percentile bands, so near-exhausted machines stand out

body.statement: The chart comes from the {{tab}} tab, where the memory chart reports {{stats}} by default.

options.text: Aggregated Charts
Top N Charts
Top N List
the average plus the 5th and 10th percentile
the average plus the 95th percentile
the average on its own
the minimum and the maximum

explanation.correct: The Aggregated Charts tab of the multi-VM Performance view is the one that charts each guest metric across the whole fleet instead of ranking individual machines, and on that tab the Available Memory chart is shipped with the average plus the 5th and 10th percentile values. That combination is what exposes the machines sitting at the low end of the memory measurement, which is what the capacity team asked for. The average plus the 95th percentile pairing belongs to the CPU Utilization % and Logical Disk Space Used % charts on the same tab, and the average on its own is the default for the two byte-rate charts, so neither of those describes the memory chart.

perChoice.tab:tab-topn: Top N Charts ranks the five worst machines for each of five metrics (CPU Utilization %, Available Memory, Logical Disk Space Used %, Bytes Sent Rate and Bytes Receive Rate); it produces a short per-metric ranking rather than one summary picture of the metric for the fleet.
perChoice.tab:tab-list: Top N List is a table of individual machines ordered by a chosen metric, starting with 20 entries and extendable to 500, so it ranks machines instead of charting the metric across the fleet.
perChoice.stats:st-avg-95: That pairing is the default for the CPU Utilization % and Logical Disk Space Used % charts on this tab; the memory chart instead adds the 5th and 10th percentile values to the average.
perChoice.stats:st-avg-only: That is the default for the two byte-rate charts, Bytes Sent Rate and Bytes Receive Rate; the memory chart also reports the 5th and 10th percentile values.
perChoice.stats:st-min-max: The memory chart does not default to the minimum and the maximum. Those two values can be picked in the percentile selector, but the shipped default for the memory chart is the average plus the 5th and 10th percentile.

body.stem: The capacity team wants a detailed look at the disk activity of one database host, db-vm-07. For that host they need the disk operations per second, the disk throughput in MB per second, the largest share of space used on any of its logical disks, and a table that lists capacity, utilization and average for each logical disk volume. The analysts report that the fleet-wide charts they normally use show none of these measures. Where should they look?

rows: One value per logical disk volume
MB per second, one value per logical disk volume
Across all logical disk volumes of the host
Capacity, utilization and average for each logical disk

options.text: Open the virtual machine and select Monitoring > Insights > Performance
Open Monitor > Solutions > Virtual Machines > Performance and stay on the Top N Charts tab
Open Monitor > Insights > Storage Accounts and select the account's Capacity workbook
Open Monitor > Solutions > Virtual Machines > Performance and stay on the Aggregated Charts tab

explanation.correct: The three extra measures the team needs — Logical Disk IOPS, Logical Disk MB/s and Max Logical Disk Used % — together with the per-logical-disk table showing capacity, utilization and average, are added only on the page scoped to a single machine, reached by opening the virtual machine and selecting Monitoring > Insights > Performance. The fleet-wide view under Monitor > Solutions exposes just the five capacity charts (CPU Utilization %, Available Memory, Logical Disk Space Used %, Bytes Sent Rate, Bytes Receive Rate) plus the Top N list, and the storage Capacity workbook reports account-level used capacity and object counts rather than the guest disk counters of a single host.

perChoice.location:b: The Top N Charts tab of the fleet-wide view only offers the five capacity charts (CPU Utilization %, Available Memory, Logical Disk Space Used %, Bytes Sent Rate, Bytes Receive Rate) with the top five machines each, so it cannot produce disk IOPS, disk MB/s, the maximum disk space used figure or a per-volume table.
perChoice.location:c: The storage account Capacity workbook reports used capacity and object counts per data service for a storage account, and it does not expose the guest disk counters of a single host or a table broken down per logical disk volume.
perChoice.location:d: Aggregated Charts show averages and percentiles for the same five fleet-wide capacity metrics, so this tab also lacks the per-machine disk IOPS, disk MB/s and maximum disk space used charts and the per-logical-disk table.

body.stem: Your network operations team works from the Network insights page in Azure Monitor, and analysts pin parts of it to the Azure dashboard that the on-call team watches. The exhibit shows the range each side is set to. Since the latest pin, the on-call team says the network figures on the dashboard cover a different period from the one the analysts picked, so the numbers no longer line up with what was seen in Network insights. Which statement explains this?

exhibit.text:
Item                                              | Value
-------------------------------------------------|---------------
Range picked by the analysts in Network insights | Last 24 hours
Time range configured on the pinned dashboard    | Last 1 hour
Dashboard that holds the pin                     | net-ops-handover

body.statement: The most accurate explanation is that {{reason}}.

options.text: the Network insights workbook uses the Auto time grain derived from the selected time range, but once a chart is pinned the time range follows the dashboard settings
the Network insights workbook uses the Auto time grain derived from the selected time range, and pinning a chart copies that range to the Azure dashboard so the period shown there stays fixed
Network insights stores a fixed grain for every chart in the workbook, so whether or not a chart is pinned makes no difference to the range or the grain that is displayed
a pinned chart follows the dashboard settings for its time range, but the grain stays at the value used in Network insights instead of being derived from the range

explanation.correct: Network insights workbooks run with the Auto time grain, and that grain is derived from the selected time range. When any part of a workbook is pinned, however, the time range depends on the dashboard settings instead. The pinned view therefore shows the period configured on the dashboard (here the last hour) and the grain derived from that period, which is why the on-call team no longer sees the 24-hour period the analysts had chosen in Network insights.

perChoice.reason:b: Pinning does not copy the range chosen in Network insights onto the dashboard. Once a chart is pinned, the period displayed comes from the dashboard settings, so it follows the dashboard and can change with it rather than staying fixed at the range the analysts picked.
perChoice.reason:c: Network insights does not use a fixed grain for its charts. It uses the Auto time grain, which is derived from the selected time range, so pinning a chart does change which period, and therefore which grain, is displayed.
perChoice.reason:d: The grain is not frozen at the value used in Network insights. The Auto time grain continues to be derived from the range in effect, and after pinning that range comes from the dashboard settings, so the grain changes along with the dashboard range instead of staying put.
